soil-agri-205.title: Why rare storms do most of the erosion damage
soil-agri-205.text: One storm can undo thirty years of care. About one-third of the water erosion damage in a field over 30 years commonly comes from a single extreme rainfall event. Wind works the same way: the 1930s Dust Bowl wind erosion followed a decade of extremely dry years. Because such events are rare, the risk is easy to underestimate, yet most erosion damage comes from them. This is a hard fact for {{ref:soil-water-001}}, which is often judged by ordinary years.

soil-agri-221.title: Land use: what people do with a parcel
soil-agri-221.text:
Every parcel of land has a job. Land use describes what people do on it, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied. The FAO defines it as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them. The IPCC defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel, and groups it into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands.

The choices matter for {{ref:soil-found-077}}, water, {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, plants and animals. Poor choices contribute to soil erosion, soil degradation, land degradation and desertification. Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland. Early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland.

Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts. An urban growth boundary is one such tool.

soil-meth-066.title: Digital image analysis: teaching computers to read pictures
soil-meth-066.text: Image analysis extracts meaningful information from images, mainly digital ones, by digital image processing. Computers are indispensable for large data and quantitative extraction, but human vision still cannot be replaced in many applications. Object-based analysis groups pixels into homogeneous objects by segmentation and then classifies them. Over-segmentation is often preferred when classifying high-resolution images. The method is applied in metallography, for instance to determine the mineral content of a rock sample.

soil-meth-064.title: Polarized light microscopy and birefringent minerals
soil-meth-064.text: Some samples shine under polarized light. Polarized light microscopy covers optical techniques that illuminate a sample with it, and works best on birefringent samples. A polarizing plate converts natural light into polarized light, and birefringent samples interact strongly with it, giving contrast against the background. The method is used extensively in optical mineralogy, the basis of identifying minerals in the {{ref:soil-meth-030}}. More complex variants include differential interference contrast and interference reflection microscopy.

soil-meth-065.title: X-ray microtomography: a 3D look without cutting
soil-meth-065.text: X-ray microtomography, or micro-CT, makes cross-sections of an object at micrometre pixel size and rebuilds a 3D model without destroying the sample. It is computed tomography in which the sample rotates while source and detector stay still, or the source and detector rotate around the specimen. Cone-beam systems use a 2D detector to record projection images, from which cross-sections are reconstructed. Stacking slices builds a volume of voxels that can be viewed in any plane, and segmentation separates structures that have similar density. In geology it is used to analyze micropores in reservoir rocks.

soil-meth-045.title: Spatial analysis: studying things by where they are
soil-meth-045.text:
Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties. It spans many methods, especially spatial statistics, and covers spatial interpolation, spatial regression and spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's I and Geary's C. Geographic information systems capture, store, manipulate and analyse spatial data, with map overlay a basic vector operation.

Two errors recur. The ecological fallacy draws conclusions about individuals from aggregate data. The locational fallacy is a poor spatial characterisation of the elements. Spatial sampling picks limited locations to measure phenomena that show dependency and heterogeneity; basic schemes are random, clustered and systematic.

soil-meth-039.title: Landsat: fifty years of Earth from orbit
soil-meth-039.text: No other program has watched Earth from space for as long. Landsat is the longest-running enterprise that has acquired satellite imagery of Earth. The first satellite launched on 23 July 1972 as the Earth Resources Technology Satellite and was renamed Landsat 1 in 1975. Landsat 9 launched on 27 September 2021. Landsat 7 data has eight spectral bands with spatial resolutions from 15 to 60 m and a temporal resolution of 16 days, and a scene is about 185 km by 185 km. Instruments progressed from the Multispectral Scanner (Landsat 1-5) to the Thematic Mapper, the Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (Landsat 7) and, on Landsat 8, the Operational Land Imager plus a Thermal Infrared Sensor. The result is one of the longest uninterrupted remote-sensing time series, from 1972 to the present, widely used for land-cover determination.

soil-agri-090.title: The scorpan model: clorpt made digital
soil-agri-090.text:
In 2003, McBratney and colleagues extended Jenny's clorpt model so that soil-environment relationships could be applied digitally. The result is the scorpan model. It keeps climate, organisms, relief, parent material and age, the {{ref:soil-form-043}} behind {{ref:soil-form-049}}, and adds two factors. The s stands for intrinsic soil properties captured by remote and proximal sensors, and n for spatial coordinates or position relative to a geographic phenomenon. A quantitative function f links individual scorpan factors, or a combination, to the soil property or class being predicted.

Its strength is flexibility. It combines existing soil surveys with remote sensing, elevation, climate, land use and geology data, all as raster layers re-projected to one projection and resolution. Relief, usually from a digital elevation model, is the most used factor in {{ref:soil-agri-089}}, soil is second, and climate is one of the least used, partly because topography proxies for local climate. Age is rarely used because soil age is hard to put into a GIS-friendly form. The position factor can use sample coordinates or distance to a feature.

Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils. Its digital techniques date from the 1970s, and technology made them practical products since the 2000s. A map needs three ingredients: environmental layers representing scorpan factors, geo-referenced soil data, and a model relating soil to environment to predict at unsampled locations. It is usually supervised learning. Sample locations are intersected with the environmental layers to build a training set, and a fitted classification or regression function is then applied to all cells, linking back to {{ref:soil-form-042}}.

soil-meth-037.title: Electromagnetic induction: a field from a changing field
soil-meth-037.text: A changing magnetic field drives a current. Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across a conductor in such a field. Faraday published its discovery in 1831, and Joseph Henry found it independently in 1832. Maxwell later described it mathematically. Faraday's law says the induced emf in a closed circuit equals the rate of change of enclosed magnetic flux, and Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it. A changing current in one wire induces an emf in a second wire within reach of its magnetic field, which is the principle of the transformer. Conductors in changing magnetic fields also develop circular eddy currents in planes perpendicular to the field.

soil-meth-050.title: Conventional soil mapping and its limits
soil-meth-050.text:
Conventional soil mapping is the surveyor-led production of soil maps from field inspections, building on Jenny's soil-forming factors and national taxonomic systems. The steps are objectives, background compilation and initial legend, then soil inspections, field mapping and correlation, and finally map production and a report. Soils are represented as a profile, a 1-3 m wide pedon, a polypedon of connected similar pedons, or a map unit, the polygon mapped by surveyors.

The method has limits. Choropleth maps assume each map unit is homogeneous, yet units contain inclusions of minor soils too small to map, and real soil change is often a fuzzy gradation rather than a sharp boundary. Raising map-unit purity raises cost exponentially. Maps made for different objectives leave mismatched boundaries and inconsistent series names across counties and provinces. Still, legacy maps hold decades of surveyor knowledge and serve as training data for digital soil maps.

soil-meth-053.title: Judging a digital soil map: accuracy assessment
soil-meth-053.text:
A digital soil map is only as good as its test against reality. Accuracy assessment measures how far predicted values differ from observed ones, using an independent validation dataset, for maps from {{ref:soil-agri-089}}. Categorical predictions use overall accuracy, the share correctly predicted, and Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement. Both range from 0 to 1.

Continuous predictions use mean square error, root mean square error (in the soil variable's units), R2 and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient. Lower MSE or RMSE means a more accurate model. R2 is not accuracy, because it ignores bias from systematic over- or underprediction. The concordance coefficient, which measures fit to the 45-degree line, is more appropriate.

soil-meth-054.title: Where digital soil map uncertainty comes from
soil-meth-054.text:
Every predicted soil map carries error, and it should be estimated as carefully as it is validated. Uncertainty in a map from {{ref:soil-agri-089}} comes from three sources: the measured soil property, the environmental predictors, and the predictive model. Property errors arise from laboratory methods, pedotransfer functions and GPS location accuracy. Predictor errors come from DEM vertical error, sensor error, and polygon boundaries and scale.

Model structure matters because linear, non-linear and hybrid models, such as model trees, capture different soil-environment relationships. International standards such as GlobalSoilMap require a 90% prediction interval map with 5% and 95% limits. A wider interval means higher uncertainty, and this applies only to continuous variables.

soil-meth-047.title: Spatial scale: how big is the space?
soil-meth-047.text: Spatial scale describes or categorises the size of a space, or the extent at which a phenomenon or process occurs. A common geography and meteorology scheme runs from micro (1 m to 1 km, local) through meso (1 to 100 km, regional) and macro (100 to 10,000 km, continental) to mega (global) and giga (superglobal). These divisions are somewhat arbitrary and shift by context, so meso and macro must be adjusted accordingly.

soil-meth-041.title: The modifiable areal unit problem
soil-meth-041.text:
Change the boundaries and the answer changes. The modifiable areal unit problem, or MAUP, is a source of statistical bias that arises when point-based measures are aggregated into areal units. Summary values depend on both the shape and the scale of the aggregation unit, so results differ between, say, state and county boundaries. The scale effect changes results between aggregation levels, and correlation generally rises as unit size rises. The zoning effect changes them when data are regrouped at the same scale.

Gehlke and Biehl first recognised the problem in 1934, and Openshaw described it in detail in 1984. It is closely related to ecological fallacy, a pitfall of {{ref:soil-meth-045}}. Aggregation can hide a strong correlation or create a spurious one, so sensitivity analysis with several areal units is recommended to estimate the uncertainty of coefficients.

soil-meth-043.title: Random forest: many trees voting
soil-meth-043.text:
Random forest is an ensemble learning method for classification and regression that builds many decision trees during training. Classification returns the class chosen by most trees. Regression returns the average of the trees' predictions, which corrects decision trees' habit of overfitting.

Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement, called bagging, and each split considers only a random subset of features. This decorrelates the trees when a few features are very strong predictors. Tin Kam Ho created the first algorithm in 1995, and Breiman and Cutler extended it. Variable importance can be ranked by permutation: permute a feature in the out-of-bag samples and see how much the error rises, or use mean decrease in impurity. The cost of higher accuracy than a single tree is lost interpretability.
